school-leaders-and-ngo-staff-ai-adoption.core: Posted in last 7 days School Leaders & NGO Staff - AI Adoption Challenges Across Sectors Everyone is talking about AI in schools. But who’s listening to school leaders? This question had been on my mind, and I am thankful to Anthropic x Global School Leaders for inviting me to their event in New York, focused on school leaders in conversations about AI and education. My policy training has taught me to be cautious about assuming that an intervention that works in one place will work just as well in another. In research, this connects to questions of external validity and policy transfer.Evidence matters, but so does context. I saw a version of this challenge in an intervention I developed, focused on school administration in Tanzania. The question was not simply if administrators could be given educational materials or training. It was whether those resources would be enough to address their needs, or whether an effective intervention would also require time, ongoing support, and a better understanding of the challenges faced in their day-to-day work. I think the same principle applies to AI in education! Having been in school when the modern AI boom happened, I know that a tool may be technically impressive, but school leaders still need to evaluate its relevance, safety, privacy implications, and educational value. Teachers need time and support to incorporate it into their work. And schools need the infrastructure and resources to use it effectively. These needs will look different across contexts, which is precisely why local input and evidence should shape implementation from the beginning. This question extends beyond education.... Which is why I’ve been interviewing NGOs about how they currently use AI. I’m working on an article bringing these perspectives together, with a focus on the realities of AI adoption in organizations working on social impact. Follow along for updates.If you work with schools, NGOs, foundations, or technology organizations, I’d love to hear what you’re seeing. 📍Anthropic office, NY with Asha Dhakad #aispecialist #educationpolicy #aigovernance #globaldevelopment #effectivealturism

founders-of-maternal-health-publications.author: Catharine Donnelly
founders-of-maternal-health-publications.core: Posted in last 7 days Founders of Maternal Health Publications - Growth Struggles & Wins Judging by the metrics alone, I should probably quit. One year ago, I said I’d “do Birthbabe” properly for 12 months. I gave myself a target of three magazines, a weekly newsletter, growing our socials. This isn’t a “we smashed every goal, it’s been like being strapped to a rocket” post. It hasn’t been that kind of year. But Birthbabe was never meant to be about me or my ego. It was always about amplifying what others are doing. So despite hating every second of typing this, I'm reluctantly proud. Here's why. Birthbabe started in 2021 as a passion project. I was deep in what I didn't yet realise was postnatal depression. Out of everything that could have pulled me through, it was a tiny creative project that kept me going. It pulled me through again during a second bout of depression after my second child. It's pretty much been my constant ever since. This year, we got to do what Birthbabe is here for, and shine a light on others: → Interviews with midwives, obstetricians, doulas, senior academics at Oxford, artists, politicians, female founders and so many more → Women's stories of matrescence, the mental load, friendships, parenting, postpartum psychosis, sepsis, baby loss, maternal mental health, birth trauma, recovery, and so many more that don't get enough air time → Midwives and the hours they're working, student midwives unable to find jobs after qualifying And along the way, we made things: → Five magazines (I promised three), with the sixth out in the next few weeks → The Peach Book: a traffic-light guide from pregnancy to postpartum, so mothers know when to care for themselves at home, when to call their midwife and when to get urgent help. There is traction. Tiny, but real. Emails almost daily from people asking to contribute. Birthbabe tagged in news stories, readers sharing our articles, a bigger community than last year. What we didn't have a year ago, and do now: a medical editor, a yoga therapy columnist and a fashion columnist. So, just like 12 months ago, I'm making a commitment: to keep going. But this time, I'm doing it in public. Here on LinkedIn, to hold myself to account. To keep going and to keep building. The mission hasn’t changed: a media brand for mothers. Because I truly believe that supporting mothers is like a rising tide that lifts all boats. If you want to join the journey, follow along. And if you're doing brilliant work in the maternity space, I want to hear about it. That's what Birthbabe is for. (And if you’ve ever grown a small publication into a globally dominating media brand, DM me too 😉) Birthbabe

They applied for shares in the SE Fruits IPO, paid in full, and have heard nothing since. When they tried to reach the lead manager directly, they got no answer. Those conversations stayed with me, and they shaped today’s story. It has now been 14 days since subscription closed. Investors still have no allotment, no refund and no listing date. While reporting, I went back to the prospectus to see who is responsible if this drags on. Two things stood out. First, if the company misses the allotment deadline, the prospectus says it pays a penalty of PKR 5,000 a day. That penalty goes to the stock exchange, not to the investors whose money is blocked. Second, the two lead managers signed a “solemn affirmation” to PSX that everything in the prospectus was true and that “nothing has been concealed.” They vouched for every word. Now investors are not getting answers. I won’t guess what is behind the delay. But a market that wants ordinary people to trust IPOs has to answer them when it matters. If you applied for this IPO, I would like to hear from you, in the comments or privately. Full story in the first comment. #PSX #IPO #InvestorProtection #CapitalMarkets #SEFruits #SECP

One of the most consistent pieces of feedback we receive from conference participants is this: "𝘞𝘦'𝘥 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘩𝘦𝘢𝘳 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨." Not just the success stories, but: The failed launches. The wrong strategic bets. The expansion plans that didn't deliver. The technology projects that didn't live up to expectations. The same message came through again in this year's Summit feedback and Q&A sessions. That's why, for EFSS 2027, I'm searching for the restaurant industry's most valuable failures: concepts that flopped, expansions that disappointed, technology projects that derailed, strategies that backfired, and decisions that taught unforgettable lessons.
